================
Date: 2026-09-17
Observer(s): Jane Doe
School: Elgin High School
Grade level: 9
Content area / subject: ELA
Period: Second
Class type: General Education
Visit occurred at the: Beginning of Lesson

PART 1 — TARGET / TAXONOMY / PACING
Lesson Standard: RL.9-10.2
Other disaggregation tag(s): cohort B
- There is a learning target that is directly from the content area standard.  [Partial]
- The content area standard is written at this level of thinking.  [Retrieval]
- The student evidence during the visit requires this level of thinking.  [Analysis]

ADOPTED CURRICULUM
- Pacing:  [ON pace]
- The learning students are experiencing is clearly grounded in the district’s adopted curriculum and grade/course-level expectations.  [3/5]
- Students are using the intended high-quality curricular materials and resources in ways that preserve the rigor and purpose of the lesson.  [4/5]
Notes: Adopted curriculum in use throughout.

TARGET/TASK ALIGNMENT
- There is clear evidence that students understand what they are learning and what successful learning/work looks like. (Teacher Clarity ES = 0.85)  [5/5]
- The tasks students are completing require the level of thinking, rigor, and evidence called for by the learning target/standard.  [2/5]
Notes: Task matched the target for most students.

PART 2 — INSTRUCTIONAL CLARITY FRAMEWORK COMPONENTS

2.1 DAILY ENGAGEMENT WITH COMPLEX TEXTS  (avg: 3.5)
- ENGAGEMENT: Students are required to make meaning from the text/content — citing evidence, questioning, analyzing, annotating, summarizing, or explaining their thinking — rather than primarily receiving the meaning from the teacher.  [4/5]
- ENGAGEMENT: Students are actively reading, writing, speaking, and/or listening to appropriately challenging, grade-level/complex text or content as part of the daily learning.  [3/5]
Notes: Students annotated a complex text.

2.2 DAILY ENGAGEMENT WITH ACADEMIC VOCABULARY  (avg: 2.5)
- VOCABULARY: Essential academic and discipline-specific vocabulary is intentionally taught and reinforced within the context of the learning. (Vocabulary Programs ES = 0.69)  [2/5]
- VOCABULARY: Students are expected to use newly learned academic vocabulary accurately in their speaking, writing, reasoning, or discussion. (Vocabulary Programs ES = 0.69)  [3/5]
Notes: Vocabulary was displayed but rarely used.

2.3 WORKSHOP MODEL OF INSTRUCTION  (avg: 4.5)
- Instruction is intentionally structured so that students move from explicit teaching/modeling into guided and increasingly independent application of the learning.  [5/5]
- Students are doing the majority of the cognitive work — reading, writing, discussing, reasoning, problem-solving, creating, or applying — rather than primarily watching or listening to the teacher.  [4/5]
Notes: Mini-lesson, work time, and share time were all visible.

2.4 ACADEMIC TEAMING  (avg: 3.0)
- Students are engaged in purposeful academic dialogue in which they explain their thinking, respond to others, ask questions, and build on or challenge ideas.  [3/5]
- The structure of collaborative learning requires individual accountability and meaningful contribution from all students — not simply students sitting or working together.  [3/5]
Notes: Roles were named but not held.

2.5 FORMATIVE ASSESSMENT  (avg: 4.5)
- The teacher is actively eliciting evidence of learning from multiple students during the lesson to determine who understands, who does not, and why.  [4/5]
- There is evidence that the teacher and/or students are using that information to adjust instruction, strategy, grouping, pacing, or next steps in learning.  [5/5]

2.6 ACTIONABLE FEEDBACK  (avg: 1.5)
- Students are receiving specific feedback tied to the learning target/success criteria that helps them understand where they are and what they need to do next. (Feedback ES = 0.50)  [2/5]
- Students are using feedback to revise, refine, correct, or improve their work or thinking during the learning process. (Feedback ES = 0.50)  [1/5]
Notes: Feedback was mostly evaluative.

2.7 CULTURALLY & LINGUISTICALLY RESPONSIVE  (avg: 5.0)
- Students’ cultural and linguistic backgrounds are reflected and drawn upon in the texts, resources, tasks, and discussion of the lesson.  [5/5]
- Targeted scaffolds and explicit language supports are in place so that all students, including multilingual learners and students with disabilities, engage meaningfully with grade-level content.  [5/5]
Notes: Scaffolds were in place for every group.

PART 3 — CONDITIONS FOR LEARNING
- Adults consistently initiate positive interactions with students — using names, greeting them, checking in, listening, and showing interest in them as individuals.  [4/5]
- Students readily approach, interact with, and seek assistance from adults, and adults respond with attention, respect, and support.  [5/5]
- Students listen to, include, help, encourage, and positively engage with one another across classrooms and common spaces.  [4/5]
- Expectations and routines are clearly communicated and consistently reinforced, and adults respond to student behavior calmly, respectfully, and in ways that preserve student dignity.  [3/5]
- Students have opportunities to contribute their ideas and perspectives, make meaningful choices, assume leadership or responsibility, and participate in decisions that affect their learning or school experience.  [5/5]
- When students are disengaged, isolated, struggling, or not meeting expectations, adults notice, approach, support, redirect, and reconnect them.  [4/5]
Notes: Warm, predictable routines.

PART 4 — WALK SUMMARY
Strengths: Every student had access to the grade-level text.
Growth areas: Move feedback from evaluative to actionable.
